---

Goal: one temperature indicator that flags surface-water supplies where warming
pushes water toward the temperatures at which cyanobacteria blooms take off
(growth optima of roughly 25 °C and above). All comparisons use the p90
(high-end) projected change.

# TERMS

From the USGS CMIP6-LOCA2 threshold metrics (Alder 2024,
<https://doi.org/10.5066/P13OV6GY>), computed with the CLIMDEX indices.

- **SU (summer days):** the number of days in a year with a maximum air
  temperature above 25 °C. Days.
- **GDD10 (growing degree days, base 10 °C):** the year's accumulated warmth
  above 10 °C, i.e. each day's mean temperature minus 10 °C, summed over the
  days warmer than 10 °C. °C-days. (The data files label it only "base 10C";
  this is the standard formula.)
- **GSL (growing season length):** the number of days between the first run of
  at least 6 days with a mean temperature above 5 °C and the first run of 6
  days below 5 °C after 1 July. Days, so it cannot exceed 365.
- **Change, p90:** for each model run, the future (2035-2065) mean minus the
  historical (1980-2010) mean; p90 is the run nearest the 90th percentile of
  those changes.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
source("setup.R")
mapviewOptions(fgb = FALSE)
```

```{r calc-exposure}
water_supplies <- get_wsd(rapid = TRUE)

temp_threshold_exp <- calc_temp_threshold_exposure(water_supplies = water_supplies,
                                                   historical = c(1980, 2010),
                                                   future = c(2035, 2065),
                                                   verbose = FALSE)

exp_sf <- water_supplies |>
  left_join(temp_threshold_exp, by = c("wsd_source_id", "park_unit"))
```

# DO THEY CORRELATE?

```{r correlation}
cor(temp_threshold_exp[, c("raw_su_change_p90",
                           "raw_gdd10_change_p90",
                           "raw_gsl_change_p90")],
    use = "complete.obs", method = "spearman")
```

No. In the 2026-11-11 run (1,425 supplies) every pair was weak to negative
(Spearman -0.34 to 0.12), so the three rank supplies differently. They respond to the
baseline climate in opposite ways:

- **GDD10** change grows with how warm a site already is (mean ~480 °C-days
  where SU is under 30 days today, ~880 where it is over 150), so it mostly
  re-ranks places that are already hot.
- **GSL** saturates: 142 supplies already have a season of 360+ days, and its
  change drops to ~1 day at the warmest sites.
- **SU** change peaks at moderate baselines (~42-49 days where 30-150 days are
  above 25 °C today) and is smaller at both the coldest (~36) and hottest
  (~29) sites.

```{r map-change}
mapview(exp_sf, zcol = "raw_su_change_p90", layer.name = "SU change p90 (days)") +
  mapview(exp_sf, zcol = "raw_gdd10_change_p90", layer.name = "GDD10 change p90 (C d)", hide = TRUE) +
  mapview(exp_sf, zcol = "raw_gsl_change_p90", layer.name = "GSL change p90 (days)", hide = TRUE)
```

# RECOMMENDATION: SU (DAYS ABOVE 25 °C)

Use **SU**. It is the only option with a threshold tied to the bloom mechanism:
it counts days above 25 °C, near the growth optima of bloom-forming
cyanobacteria, so a change in SU is a change in bloom-favourable days. Its
pattern also fits an exposure indicator: it is largest where supplies are newly
crossing into that range, which is where bloom risk is emerging. GDD10 has no
threshold and mostly rewards heat that already exists, and GSL measures the
general growing season (above 5 °C) and runs out of room at a tenth of the
supplies.

Limits: SU is air, not water, temperature; it applies to surface-water sources
only; and nutrients, not temperature, are the main driver of blooms. SU change
is small at the hottest sites because they are already above 25 °C most of the
year.
